text:
Recent work supports testing diagnostic reliability through controlled mutations and metamorphic relations. A [2024 recommender-system study](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2024.107410) evaluated six relations across LibRec, PREA and Surprise, finding that output relationships can reveal defects without exact recommendation labels. Earlier [ML mutation-testing experiments](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3082144/) showed that plausible cross-validation results alone can miss implementation faults. [Time to Split (RecSys 2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748164) highlights temporal leakage in sequential recommendation; preserving per-user chronology does not necessarily prevent leakage across the global timeline. These findings motivate diagnostic checks, while the benchmark’s supplied splits remain fixed.

Proposed application—not a published, validated NextItNet toolkit: inject one defect at a time into disposable copies of the single fitted model: count-minus-one readout on left-padded histories, future-token access, inconsistent item-ID mapping, and scorer/predictor mismatch. Verify that each mutation actually changes the intended behavior before counting detection. Pair these with valid controls: batch permutation, candidate permutation with corresponding score reordering, and checkpoint reload equivalence; arbitrary history permutation or extra padding need not preserve predictions. Report per-fault sensitivity = detected active faults / active faults, false-positive rate = alarms / clean-control cases, and specificity = 1 − false-positive rate, with counts and uncertainty. Use controlled future-token perturbations to check causal-prefix invariance and compare training-side versus exported-predictor scores. Keep thresholds separate from evaluation cases and all mutated copies outside inference; probe calibration establishes detection capability, not improved validation HR@10.
